# TraceCite

> TraceCite is a format and a reader for evidence-first documents. A document is one tree of blocks (section, paragraph, sentence, citation, exact quote). Every sentence opens, in place, to the exact words its sources used, the passage those words sit in, notes, tags and who checked them. Documents travel as `.trace.zip` packages, and one self-contained `trace-reader.html` opens them in any browser.

When you write a TraceCite document, quote sources verbatim by copying, with the whole passage around each quote. Never invent sources, quotes or comments. Say how far each record is checked, and label interpretation as interpretation. Record agents as agents. Validate the document before you finish.

## Start here

- [Writing with agents](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/writing-with-agents.md): heuristics for writing a document that keeps the format's promise
- [Agent skill (SKILL.md)](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/SKILL.md): the full skill, with the builder, the reader and the rules
- [Sample document](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/sample.md): one small document that uses every part, with its .bib and .trace.zip layout

## Format

- [TraceCite 1.0 specification](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/format.md): blocks, tags, sources, span tags, connected highlights, links and interactives
- [JSON Schema](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/schema/tracecite-1.0.schema.json): draft 2020-12, `tracecite/1.0`
- [BibTrace](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/bibtrace.md): BibTeX plus trace-* fields for exact quotes, passages and provenance
- [Packages (.trace.zip)](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/package.md): the manifest, the version history and how documents are opened

## Edits

- [Edits protocol](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/docs/edits.md): models stream suggested edits into an open page through `window.TraceLive`; readers accept, reject or comment. On every run, first read `TraceLive.decisions` (what was accepted, rejected or commented), then the open requests in `TraceLive.inbox`, before writing anything. Only sentences are editable. Name yourself as an agent. Every edit is a suggestion the reader accepts or rejects.

## Tools

- [trace-reader.html (latest release)](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/releases/latest/download/trace-reader.html): one file that opens any .trace.zip, with no install
- [Builder](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/scripts/build-reading.mjs): `node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data doc.trace.json --out doc.html --zip doc.trace.zip`
- [Validator](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/blob/main/scripts/validate-trace.mjs): `node scripts/validate-trace.mjs doc.trace.json`

## Optional

- [Full guidance in one file](https://prajwalsouza.github.io/TraceCite/llms-full.txt): this file's documents inlined
- [Examples](https://prajwalsouza.github.io/TraceCite/): two example papers and the sample, live

<!-- docs/writing-with-agents.md -->

# Writing TraceCite documents with an agent

A TraceCite document makes one promise: **every claim opens to the exact words
it rests on, and says how far those words were checked.** These heuristics
keep that promise when an AI agent writes or edits a document. They are about
spirit more than rules. When a case is not covered, ask which choice keeps a
reader able to check the claim.

## Evidence

- **Quote exactly, by copying.** Copy each quote programmatically from the
  source, with the whole passage it sits in (`trace-quote` and
  `trace-quote-context`). Never retype a quote or rebuild it from memory. A
  passage must contain its quote word for word. The validator rejects a quote
  with no passage unless a reason is given (`-context-withheld`).
- **Never invent.** No made-up sources, quotes, page numbers, comments or
  reviewers. A source you could not open keeps no quote: it stays "Reference
  only" and shows as unchecked.
- **Say how far each record is checked.** Use `trace-status`, `trace-checked`
  and `trace-url-read`. Unchecked stays visibly unchecked.
- **Locate quotes honestly.** Use sections and paragraph positions for web
  pages. Use page numbers only when you read the page.

## Claims

- **Label interpretation as interpretation.** A sentence that is your synthesis
  carries a role such as "Our interpretation". Its review says what the sources
  do and do not support.
- **Keep support separate from role.** Every sentence has a support decision
  (quoted, reference only, no source needed), apart from what it does
  (definition, claim, history).
- **A trace is not proof.** It shows where a claim came from. It does not show
  that the claim is true.

## Provenance

- **Agents are agents.** Record who added and checked each part: "AI agent
  (review)", "script (verbatim check)". Never present an agent as a person.
- **Sign comments as what they are.** Never write comments in a real person's
  name.

## Copyright

- **Before publishing,** keep each quoted passage within what its licence
  allows. W3C, CC BY and CC0 passages are usually fine. Journal pages often are
  not. Otherwise give a short quote, withhold the passage with a reason, and
  link to it.

## Structure

- **The tag is the schema.** A paragraph tagged `env-definition` is a
  definition, with `Label` and `Name` fields. Subsections are nested sections.
- **Comments are blocks:** `note` blocks with `Comment by`, placed under what
  they are about. Replies sit under them.
- **One tree.** Do not duplicate text across branches. Use tags and citations
  to connect ideas.

## Connected highlights, span tags and links

- **Highlights are threads, not decoration.** Use two to four, never more than
  five. Mark the first mention and the key later ones, above all where a
  different word names the same thing ("the data" for x). Colour is never the
  only signal: the words must still say what they mean.
- **Spans** (`[words]{.tag-id}`) go in your own text, never inside quotes.
  Give maths symbols a tag's `symbols` list instead of marking every formula.
- **Links** go in your own text: `[text](https://…)`, or
  `[text](#/at/block-id)` to point within the document. Every link becomes a
  tag, so add one only where a reader would want to follow it.

## Editing an open page

- **Read what already happened first.** On every run, first read `TraceLive.decisions` (what was accepted, rejected or commented), then the open requests in `TraceLive.inbox`, before writing anything. Only sentences are editable. Name yourself as an agent. Every edit is a suggestion the reader accepts or rejects. See [edits.md](edits.md).

## Interactives

- **Compute what you draw.** Derive every shape from the settings and the
  definitions. Never place things by hand.
- **Use theme classes only** (`v-…`, `f-…`, `t-…`, and `api.tagClass`), so
  every theme works. Amber and red are for problems.
- **Keep them simple.** One idea per figure. The caption says what to do and
  what to notice.

## Before you finish

1. Validate: `node scripts/validate-trace.mjs doc.trace.json` should show no
   errors, and warnings should be understood.
2. Build or open the page, and check it shows the document with no console
   errors.
3. Open one sentence all the way down: its citation, the exact quote, where it
   sits, and the passage. Check that the words match the source.
4. Export the `.trace.zip`, and note what changed (`--note`) so the version
   history says why.

See [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) for the full agent skill, [format.md](format.md)
for the format, and [sample.md](sample.md) for a document that uses every part.


---

<!-- docs/format.md -->

# TraceCite 1.0 specification

A TraceCite document is one tree. Open a sentence to see the evidence under it.
The public format identifier is `tracecite/1.0`. The schema is
[schema/tracecite-1.0.schema.json](../schema/tracecite-1.0.schema.json), using
JSON Schema draft 2020-12.

The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY express requirements, recommendations and
options. A conforming document MUST satisfy the schema and the semantic rules
below. The dependency-free validator checks core structure and semantic rules;
it is not a general JSON Schema implementation.

## Top-level fields

| Field | Shape and meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `format` | Required. `"tracecite/1.0"` for this specification. |
| `version` | Required. The number `2`. This is the storage revision the Trace reader expects, separate from `format`. |
| `id` | Optional stable document id. Set it when a title may change. The reader uses the title if no id is given. |
| `title` | Required non-empty string, at most 2,000 characters. |
| `subtitle` | Optional string under the title. |
| `authors` | Optional array of name strings or objects: `{ "name": "Ada Example", "affiliations": ["a1"], "email": "ada@example.org", "orcid": "0000-0000-0000-0000", "corresponding": true, "note": "Author note" }`. Only `name` is required in an object. |
| `affiliations` | Optional array of `{ "id": "a1", "name": "Example Institute", "country": "Country" }`. `id` and `name` are required. Authors link to ids. |
| `date` | Optional display string, normally `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `revision` | Optional display string, such as `Draft 2`. This is a document revision, separate from the format and storage versions. |
| `doi` | Optional document DOI string. |
| `license` | Optional document licence string. It describes the document, not the software. |
| `keywords` | Optional array of strings. |
| `tagTree` | Required array of tag definitions. It is the document's tag schema. |
| `parameters` | Optional tree of numeric or category measures. See below. |
| `blocks` | Required array of blocks, in reading order. |
| `sources` | Required array of shared source records. It may be empty when a bibliography supplies them. |
| `bibliography` | Optional BibTrace path, or array of paths, relative to the data file. Entries are loaded before validation. A matching entry id replaces an inline source. |
| `links` | Optional. `{ "off": true }` leaves out the generated Links tag family (see Links below). |
| `interactiveScripts` | Optional array of script paths, relative to the data file, that register interactive components (see Interactives below). `vizScripts` is the older name and is still accepted. |
| `mathTags` | Optional object controlling generated math tags: `groups` maps group names to symbol arrays; `labels` maps symbols to descriptions; `minSentences` defaults to `2`; `exclude` is a symbol array; `off: true` disables generation. |
| `documentStructure` | Optional structure-import metadata: `version`, `sourceHash`, `documentClass` strings and an `environments` string array. Rendering roles are defined by block tags and fields, not this metadata alone. |

Other supported top-level fields are `eyebrow` (a short label above the title),
`updatedAt` (an ISO date-time string), `note` (a string), `flow` and `crossRefs`.
`flow` accepts `families` (root tag ids to analyse) and `minTransitions` (a positive
integer, default `3`). `crossRefs: { "off": true }` disables generated
cross-reference tags and links. Unknown extension properties are allowed by the
schema, but a reader need not preserve or display them. The HTML builder keeps
only the fields needed by its reader and resolves bibliography data into sources.

## Blocks

Every block MUST contain these fields:

```json
{
  "id": "sentence-1",
  "type": "sentence",
  "text": "The claim as written.",
  "tags": ["role-claim"],
  "fields": [{ "key": "Added by", "value": "AI agent (example author)" }],
  "collapsed": true,
  "children": []
}
```

`collapsed` is optional. Every other property shown is required. `id` matches
`^[A-Za-z0-9_.:-]{1,160}$` and MUST be unique among blocks. `text` is a string.
`tags` contains tag ids. Each `fields` item has exactly two string properties,
`key` and `value`. Field names are case-sensitive. Authors SHOULD use a field key
only once in a record. Unknown field keys can hold extra metadata.
`children` is another array of blocks. It can continue to any depth.

| Type | Use and recognised fields |
| --- | --- |
| `section` | Heading and nested sections. `Heading level` is a string number, normally `2` through `6`. |
| `paragraph` | Groups sentences. It may also carry a structural or environment tag. An environment reads `Label` and optional `Name`. |
| `sentence` | One unit of prose. Optional `Sentence review` and `Status` explain its evidence or limits. |
| `citation` | Links to a shared source using `Source ID`. Its children can include a reference. |
| `reference` | Detailed source link using `Source ID`. `Exact supporting extract` selects the wording used here; `Relation to this sentence` explains how it supports this claim. The shared source holds quote contexts. |
| `note` | A note under any block, with further notes as children. A `Comment by` field, even with an empty value, makes it a comment; `Commented on` gives its date. Replies are child comments. |
| `figure` | Label in `text`. `Assets` is a JSON array encoded as a string, such as `["figures/tree.svg"]`. `Video asset`, `Video poster` and `Figure layout` are optional. Add a caption paragraph as a child. Supported images are embedded by the builder; videos are left out of the reading page. |
| `table` | Contains `table-row` children. Captions and table notes can also be children. `Table storage: cell-blocks-v1` marks cell-block storage. Legacy `Rows` data is supported by the vendored reader; new documents SHOULD use cell blocks. |
| `table-row` | MUST be a child of `table`. `Table header: yes` marks the header. For cell-block rendering, put exactly one header row first. |
| `table-cell` | MUST be a child of `table-row`. The cell's content is its `text`; evidence can be attached below it. |

Any block can carry `Added by`, `Added via` and `Added on` fields. These describe
who added it, how, and when. Mark agents and scripts honestly. A recorded check
is a provenance claim, not a guarantee that the evidence is correct.

Figure asset paths use `images/` or `figures/` below `assets/manuscript/`, next to
the data file. The validator permits PNG, JPEG, SVG and PDF paths and forbids
`..`. The reading builder embeds PNG, JPEG and SVG images; a PDF is not an
embedded figure. `Video poster` names a poster image. The builder can also look
for assets in the vendored Trace folder.

## Tags are a schema

Each tag is `{ "id": "role", "name": "Sentence role", "children": [] }`.
Children have the same shape. An optional `collapsed` boolean controls the
initial disclosure. Ids match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$` and MUST be unique across
the entire tag tree. Names are non-empty strings of at most 120 characters.
A block's tags, source tags and `Quote tags` MUST name defined tags. Unknown tags
are errors. An ancestor tag includes the tags beneath it when reading in focus.

Root tags define families. Conventional families are `role`, `support`, `topic`
and `revision`. They receive the reader's blue, amber, green and plum colours.
An author can define other families.

Some tags have rendering meaning. Under a `document-structure` family, the
reader recognises `ordered-item`, `unordered-item`, `description-item`, `heading`,
`figure`, `table`, `caption`, `table-note`, `abstract`, `quote`, `code-block`,
`equation` and `accessible-description`. These tags MUST still be defined in
`tagTree`. List fields include `List group`, `List depth`, `List start`,
`List number` and `List label`. Their values are strings.

A paragraph tagged `env-lemma` is a lemma. The same rule covers `env-theorem`,
`env-proposition`, `env-corollary`, `env-definition`, `env-remark`, `env-example`,
`env-conjecture`, `env-claim`, `env-assumption` and `env-proof`. `Label` supplies
its number; `Name` supplies an optional name. Sentences below it carry the
statement or proof steps. The builder and CLI validator add the `env` family
and the used environment tags before validation. A caller of the exported
`validate()` function MUST call `ensureEnvironmentTags()` first for that shorthand.

The builder reserves `math` and `math-*` for generated mathematics tags, `xref`
and `xref-*` for cross-references, `provenance` and `prov-*` for provenance, and
`comments` and `comments-*` for comments. Authors SHOULD leave these names free.
The builder rejects an existing generated root when it needs to add that family.
Math and cross-reference generation can be switched off with the options above.
The generated families and indexes are added to the built page; they do not
rewrite the input JSON.

## Span tags and connected highlights

A span tag marks part of a text with a tag. It uses Pandoc's bracketed-span
syntax, so it exports cleanly:

```text
The input is a [list of n numbers]{.hl-x}.
```

Spans work in block text, headings, captions and notes. They never go inside
exact quotes or their passages, which stay verbatim. The tag id must be in
`tagTree`; an unknown id is an error, as for block tags. A block that contains
a span also carries the span's tag, so every block-level tag feature keeps
working, and tag focus lights up exactly the spans. In formulas, use MathJax's
own `\class{hl-x}{x}`.

**Connected highlights** are one use of span tags: threads that a reader can
follow by colour across words, symbols, headings and figures. By convention
they sit in a tag family `connected`. A tag has two optional properties:

| Property | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `slot` | 1 to 5: one of five theme-aware colours. Spans with the tag take it as a soft tint and text colour. |
| `symbols` | TeX symbols, such as `"q"` or `"\\mu"`, coloured automatically in every formula. Each one becomes `\class{<tag>}{…}` when the page is prepared. The data file is not changed. |

```json
{ "id": "connected", "name": "Connected highlights", "children": [
  { "id": "hl-q", "name": "q, the power", "slot": 1, "symbols": ["q"], "children": [] },
  { "id": "hl-x", "name": "x, the data", "slot": 2, "symbols": ["x"], "children": [] } ] }
```

Words are never coloured automatically: writers mark them with spans. These
are the author's judgement, unlike the automatic maths tags, which tag every
symbol mechanically. A highlight need not be maths: "paracetamol" in the text
and a tablet drawn in the same colour in an interactive are one thread.
Interactives get a tag's colour with `api.tagColor(id)` or
`api.tagClass(id, 'stroke' | 'fill' | 'text')`.

Readers choose how they look under Settings → Reading → Connected highlights: **Text colour** (the default), **Highlighted** (adds a soft tint) or **Off** (ink only). Tag focus tints the focused spans in every style.

Use them sparingly:

- At most five threads; usually two to four.
- Mark the first mention and the key later ones, especially where a different
  word refers to the same thing ("the data" for x).
- Colour is never the only signal: the words still say what they are.
- A thread keeps its slot in every theme.

## Links

```text
See [the W3C spec](https://www.w3.org/TR/html401/), or [the definition](#/at/p-def).
```

`[text](https://…)`, `http://` and `mailto:` links open in a new tab, and
bare `https://` addresses become links too. `[text](#/at/<block id>)` jumps
to that block within the document. Nothing else becomes a link: other schemes
(`javascript:`, `data:` and the rest) stay plain text, and the validator warns
about them. Links work wherever span tags do, and never inside exact quotes.
They are never underlined. External ones end in a small arrow and show their
address on hover. Clicking a link never opens the sentence around it.

Links are also tags. When the page is prepared, a generated **Links** family
tags every block that links out:

- **External link**, with one child per site (for example `w3.org`);
- **Internal link**;
- **Email**.

The tag tree can then light up every line that links somewhere. The data file
is not changed, and `"links": { "off": true }` leaves the family out.

## Parameters

A parameter has `id`, `name`, optional `measure`, `plot`, `unit` and `children`.
`measure` is `characters`, `words`, `citations`, `quotes`, or an object such as
`{ "field": "Confidence" }` for a number and
`{ "field": "Method", "type": "category" }` for text. `type: "number"` is also
accepted. Parent rows can group child parameters without their own measure.

`plot` is `histogram`, `strip`, `counts` or `categories`. Without a plot, text
uses categories, whole numbers spanning at most eight use counts, and other
numbers use a histogram. Without `parameters`, the reader supplies Length
(characters and words) and Evidence (citations and checked quotes). Filtering
changes the reading view, not the document's data.

## Sources and quotes

A source has `id`, `type: "source"`, `text` and `fields`. Optional properties are
`tags`, `collapsed` and `children`. Source ids follow the block id syntax and
MUST be unique among sources. A `Source ID` field MUST resolve to a source after
bibliographies have been loaded. The usual path is sentence → citation →
reference → shared source fields. Exact quotes and contexts are stored as
fields, not as extra block types.

| Source field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `APA citation`, `First author`, `Year`, `APA reference` | Citation label and reference text. |
| `URL`, `DOI` | Source location and identifier. |
| `Bib key`, `Bib data` | Bibliography key and structured bibliography data encoded as a JSON string. Used to restyle citations. |
| `Record status` | How far this source has been checked. A source without a checked passage SHOULD say `Reference only` and carry no invented quote. |
| `Checked on`, `Page read`, `Note` | Record check date, page actually read and a general note. |
| `Added by`, `Added via`, `Added on` | Record provenance. Dates normally use `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `Exact quote`, `Exact quote 2`, … | Source wording, copied verbatim. Quote 1 has no numeric suffix. |
| `Quote location`, `Quote location 2`, … | Where that quote sits: section, paragraph, page or line. |
| `Quote context`, `Quote context 2`, … | The full passage containing that quote, copied verbatim. It MUST contain the quote as an exact substring. |
| `Quote context withheld`, `Quote context withheld 2`, … | A non-empty reason for omitting the passage, such as copyright. Use this when the context cannot be reproduced. |
| `Quote tags`, `Quote tags 2`, … | Semicolon-separated tag ids from `tagTree`. |
| `Quote note.1`, `Quote note.2`, `Quote note 2.1`, … | Notes on quote 1, then on quote 2. The final number is the note number. |
| `Quote note by.1`, `Quote note by 2.1`, … | Who wrote that note. |
| `Quote comment.1`, `Quote comment 2.1`, … | Comments on a quote. |
| `Quote comment by.1`, `Quote comment by 2.1`, … | Comment authors; empty means unsigned. |
| `Quote added by`, `Quote added via`, `Quote checked by`, `Quote checked on` | Quote provenance. Append ` 2`, ` 3`, … for later quotes. There is no per-quote added-date field in the current BibTrace converter. |

Copy quotes and contexts from the source. Do not repair wording, punctuation or
math. Notes interpret the evidence separately. A context SHOULD be the full
paragraph or other meaningful passage, not an unrelated surrounding slice.
Each non-empty quote MUST have its context or an explicit withholding reason.
When both fields are supplied, any supplied context MUST still contain the quote.
Check separately that a quote and its passage actually occur in the source.
The validator cannot check that external fact or decide whether a passage is
complete or its reproduction is permitted.

## Validation and building

```sh
node scripts/validate-trace.mjs examples/outliners.trace.json
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data examples/outliners.trace.json --out out.html
```

The CLI loads bibliography entries and environment definitions before checking.
The builder does the same and stops on errors. Errors include missing core
fields, a storage revision other than `2`, duplicate block, source or tag ids,
unknown block types or tags, unresolved source links, invalid table nesting,
unsafe figure paths, invalid parameter choices, invalid Flow family ids, and
missing or mismatched quote contexts. The format check warns for a missing
`format` for compatibility with older Trace data. It rejects malformed format
identifiers and other major versions, including `tracecite/2.0`. The 1.0 schema
requires `format: "tracecite/1.0"`; the CLI accepts other `1.x` or `1.x.y`
identifiers but does not implement future features merely by accepting them.

Warnings cover quotes over 40 words, missing quote locations, missing asset
files, figures without media and unbalanced math delimiters. A warning is not a
licence decision or a completed source check. Schema validation and semantic
validation complement each other: JSON Schema checks field shapes; the script
checks relationships, exact context inclusion and local asset paths.

Block text and field values may contain inline markdown. Math accepts
`\( … \)` or `$ … $` inline and `\[ … \]` or `$$ … $$` for display. Store the
backslashes as normal JSON string escapes. The builder embeds the document and
reading code by default. `--data-url name.json` instead writes data beside the
page for fetching over HTTP. That option needs a server. Neither build changes
the source JSON. Runtime fonts and MathJax may need network access.

## Local reading state

Reading position is local browser state. It MUST NOT be stored in the document.
The key is `trace-position:<id>`, falling back to the title when `id` is absent:

```text
{ "v": 1, "block": "sentence-1", "section": "section-1", "offset": 0, "at": "2026-11-24T12:00:00.000Z" }
```

`block` and `section` identify the reading place; `offset` gives the position
within it in pixels; `at` is the save time as an ISO date-time string. The local record's `v` is its own revision.
An explicit `#/at/<block id>` address takes precedence over a saved position.
Themes, filters and measured chunk heights are also reader state, separate from
source evidence and authorship.

## Versioning

The format uses semantic versions: major.minor.patch. This specification is
1.0.0, identified in documents as `tracecite/1.0` (patch zero is implicit).
Additive changes are minor. Breaking changes require a new major version.
Clarifications and compatible fixes are patch changes. A document declares the
format version it was written for. The storage field `version: 2` and the
software release `0.1.0` are separate version sequences.

## Interactives

An interactive is a live figure. A `figure` block becomes one when it has an
`Interactive` field naming a component, and optionally an
`Interactive settings` field holding JSON. The older names `Viz` and
`Viz settings` are still accepted.

```json
{ "id": "fig-tug", "type": "figure", "text": "Figure 2. The tug of war",
  "tags": [], "collapsed": false, "children": [],
  "fields": [{ "key": "Interactive", "value": "tug-of-war" },
             { "key": "Interactive settings", "value": "{\"data\":[1,2,4]}" }] }
```

Components are scripts that call `TraceViz.register(name, draw)`; `api.tagColor(id)` and `api.tagClass(id, kind)` give a connected highlight's colour, so a figure's line for x matches x in the text. A document
lists its scripts in `interactiveScripts`, and they travel inside its
`.trace.zip` (see [package.md](package.md)). An interactive figure needs no
`Assets`. The hook is deliberately small: anything a script can draw, a
document can bring. Interactives use theme classes rather than fixed colours,
so they follow the reader's theme.


---

<!-- docs/bibtrace.md -->

# BibTrace

BibTrace is BibTeX plus `trace-*` fields. A source record can travel with its
exact quotes, their context passages, notes, tags and provenance. Ordinary
bibliography tools can ignore the extra fields.

## Use a bibliography

Set `"bibliography": "refs.bib"` in a TraceCite data file. The path is relative
to that file. An array loads several files in order. The builder also accepts
`--bib refs.bib`, resolved relative to the data file. Citation and reference
blocks link through a `Source ID` field whose value is the BibTeX entry key.
Loaded entries replace inline sources with the same id; later files win.
The document still needs a `sources` array, which may be empty.

`scripts/bibtrace.mjs` exports `parseBib`, `writeBib`, `bibToSources`,
`loadBibliography` and `delatex`. It handles braced and quoted values,
`@string` definitions, `#` concatenation and common LaTeX accents. Trace evidence
fields preserve their wording; ordinary bibliographic text is normalised for
display. This is a small parser, not a full TeX processor.

## Fields on each record

| BibTeX field | Meaning | Trace source field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Standard fields: `author`, `editor`, `title`, `journal`, `shortjournal`, `booktitle`, `volume`, `number`, `pages`, `year`, `month`, `day`, `doi`, `url`, `eprint`, `archiveprefix`, `publisher`, `institution`, `organization`, `howpublished`, `shorthand`, and others | Ordinary bibliography data. `shorthand` overrides the author–date label. | Preserved in `Bib data`; the converter computes `APA citation`, `First author`, `Year`, `APA reference`, `URL` and `DOI`. The entry key becomes the source id and `Bib key`. |
| `trace-status` | How far the record has been checked. Set this explicitly. Without it, the converter labels a record with a first quote `Checked excerpt`, otherwise `Reference only · no passage checked`. That default is not an independent verification. | `Record status` |
| `trace-checked` | Date checked, normally `YYYY-MM-DD`. | `Checked on` |
| `trace-url-read` | The page actually read. | `Page read` |
| `trace-note` | A general note about this record. | `Note` |
| `trace-added-by` | Person or agent that added the record. | `Added by` |
| `trace-added-via` | How it arrived: manual, Zotero, agent, script, PDF, web page, etc. | `Added via` |
| `trace-added-on` | Date added. | `Added on` |

## Fields on each quote n

Quote 1 has no numeric suffix: `trace-quote`, `trace-quote-context`, etc.
For quote 2, insert `-2` after `quote`: `trace-quote-2`,
`trace-quote-2-context`, etc. Continue with `-3`, `-4`, and so on.
In the table, `[-n]` means that optional suffix. It is not literal text.
`m` is a note or comment number, starting at 1.

| BibTrace field | Meaning | Trace source field for quote 1 / quote 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trace-quote[-n]` | Exact words from a checked source. | `Exact quote` / `Exact quote 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-location` | Section, paragraph, page or line. | `Quote location` / `Quote location 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-context` | Full passage around the quote, verbatim. It must contain the exact quote. | `Quote context` / `Quote context 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-context-withheld` | Non-empty reason why that passage is omitted. Required when no context is supplied. | `Quote context withheld` / `Quote context withheld 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-tags` | Semicolon-separated tag ids, defined in the document's tag tree. | `Quote tags` / `Quote tags 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-note-m` | A note interpreting or qualifying the quote. | `Quote note.1` / `Quote note 2.1` for note 1 |
| `trace-quote[-n]-note-m-by` | Who wrote the note. | `Quote note by.1` / `Quote note by 2.1` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-comment-m` | A comment on the quote. | `Quote comment.1` / `Quote comment 2.1` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-comment-m-by` | Comment author; optional, empty means unsigned. | `Quote comment by.1` / `Quote comment by 2.1` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-added-by` | Who added the quote. | `Quote added by` / `Quote added by 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-added-via` | How the quote arrived. | `Quote added via` / `Quote added via 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-checked-by` | Who checked the quote. | `Quote checked by` / `Quote checked by 2` |
| `trace-quote[-n]-checked-on` | Date of that check. | `Quote checked on` / `Quote checked on 2` |

The older location spelling `trace-quote-location-2` is also read, but the
preferred spelling is `trace-quote-2-location`. There is no per-quote
`trace-quote-added-on` field in this converter; use record `trace-added-on` and
quote `trace-quote-checked-on` for their respective dates.

Number quotes, notes and comments consecutively. The current converter reads
numbers 1 through 49 and stops at the first missing later quote, note or comment.
It can read quote 2 when quote 1 is absent, but authors should start at 1.

A quote must be copied from its source. Copy its context too, or state why that
passage is withheld. The validator rejects missing contexts and passages that
do not contain their quote. It cannot verify an external source or infer that
a check really happened. Do not call an unread source checked. Use honest
labels such as `AI agent (example author)` and `script (verbatim check)` when
those are who performed the work.

## Complete record

This is the complete W3C HTML record from
[examples/bibtrace-example.bib](../examples/bibtrace-example.bib). It has two
quotes from the same passage. Each quote keeps its own location and note. The
`topic-markup` tag must exist in the document that imports this record.

```bibtex
@techreport{raggett1999html,
  author                   = {Raggett, Dave and Le Hors, Arnaud and Jacobs, Ian},
  title                    = {{HTML} 4.01 Specification},
  institution              = {World Wide Web Consortium},
  type                     = {W3C Recommendation},
  year                     = {1999},
  url                      = {https://www.w3.org/TR/html401/intro/intro.html},
  trace-quote              = {HTML has its roots in SGML which has always been a language for the specification of structural markup.},
  trace-quote-location     = {2.4.1 Separate structure and presentation · first sentence},
  trace-quote-context      = {HTML has its roots in SGML which has always been a language for the specification of structural markup. As HTML matures, more and more of its presentational elements and attributes are being replaced by other mechanisms, in particular style sheets. Experience has shown that separating the structure of a document from its presentational aspects reduces the cost of serving a wide range of platforms, media, etc., and facilitates document revisions.},
  trace-quote-tags         = {topic-markup},
  trace-quote-note-1       = {The quote is the first sentence of its passage, so the passage starts with it.},
  trace-quote-checked-by   = {script (verbatim check)},
  trace-quote-checked-on   = {2026-11-24},
  trace-quote-2            = {Experience has shown that separating the structure of a document from its presentational aspects reduces the cost of serving a wide range of platforms},
  trace-quote-2-location   = {2.4.1 Separate structure and presentation · third sentence},
  trace-quote-2-context    = {HTML has its roots in SGML which has always been a language for the specification of structural markup. As HTML matures, more and more of its presentational elements and attributes are being replaced by other mechanisms, in particular style sheets. Experience has shown that separating the structure of a document from its presentational aspects reduces the cost of serving a wide range of platforms, media, etc., and facilitates document revisions.},
  trace-quote-2-note-1     = {Two quotes may share one passage; each marks its own words in it.},
  trace-added-via          = {web page},
  trace-added-on           = {2026-11-24},
  trace-status             = {Checked excerpt · quotes checked verbatim against the page text},
  trace-checked            = {2026-11-24},
  trace-url-read           = {https://www.w3.org/TR/html401/intro/intro.html},
}
```

That bibliography also includes W3C XML and TEI P5 excerpts, plus a reference-only
book record. See [NOTICE.md](../NOTICE.md) for passage credits and licences.

<!-- docs/package.md -->

# TraceCite packages (`.trace.zip`)

A package holds one TraceCite document and everything it needs, in one file.
It is a plain zip, so any zip tool can open it. Reading pages carry their
package, `trace-reader.html` opens any package, and Export hands one back.

## Contents

```text
outliners.trace.zip
├─ manifest.json              what is in the package, and its version history
├─ outliners.trace.json       the trace data, exactly as written
├─ refs.bib                   BibTrace sources (optional)
├─ assets/manuscript/…        figure images (optional)
└─ my-interactive.js          interactive components (optional)
```

Paths keep their places relative to the data file, as on disk, so the data is
never rewritten. A path may not leave that folder (`..`) or be absolute.

## manifest.json

```json
{
  "format": "tracecite/1.0",
  "package": 1,
  "version": 2,
  "title": "Outlines you can read",
  "data": "outliners.trace.json",
  "bibliography": ["refs.bib"],
  "assets": ["assets/manuscript/figures/timeline.svg"],
  "interactiveScripts": ["my-interactive.js"],
  "files": [{ "path": "outliners.trace.json", "bytes": 61234 }],
  "history": [
    { "version": 1, "date": "2026-11-24T18:30:01.320Z", "note": "First package",
      "hash": "sha256:2cb0…", "previous": null },
    { "version": 2, "date": "2026-11-25T09:00:00.000Z", "by": "Ada Example", "note": "Sharper subtitle",
      "hash": "sha256:c28e…", "previous": "sha256:2cb0…" }
  ],
  "generator": "TraceCite build-reading"
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `format` | Required. The TraceCite format version, `tracecite/1.x`. A reader rejects another major version. |
| `package` | Required. The package layout version, `1`. |
| `version` | The document's own version: the latest entry in `history`. It is separate from `format`. |
| `title` | The document's title, for file names and listings. |
| `data` | Required. The path of the trace data file. |
| `bibliography` | BibTrace files to load, in order. Entries replace inline sources with the same id. |
| `assets` | Figure images named in `Assets` and `Video poster` fields, under `assets/manuscript/`. |
| `interactiveScripts` | Interactive components named in the data's `interactiveScripts` (or the older `vizScripts`). |
| `files` | Every file except the manifest, with its size in bytes. |
| `history` | The document's versions, oldest first. See below. |
| `label` | Optional eyebrow label above the title, if the data has no `eyebrow`. |
| `generator` | What wrote the package. |

## Version history

Each entry in `history` records one version of the document's content:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | 1, 2, 3, … |
| `date` | When this version was made (ISO 8601). |
| `by` | Who made it (optional). |
| `note` | What changed (optional). |
| `hash` | `sha256:` of the data file and its `.bib` files, in path order. |
| `previous` | The previous entry's hash, or `null` for the first. |

A new entry is added only when the hash changes. Comparing the hashes of two
exports tells you whether their content differs. The builder carries the
history over from the last package it wrote for the document: the `--zip`
file, the page being rebuilt, or `--history old.trace.zip`. Use `--by` and
`--note` to sign and describe the new entry. Rebuilding unchanged data gives
the same bytes. A reading page never edits its document, so Export hands back
the package as it was opened. A document opened from loose files gets its
first entry when it is packed.

The reader shows the history under Settings → Document.

## Opening a document

Any reading page opens a document dropped anywhere on it, or chosen under
Settings → Document → Import. The standalone reader also has **Choose a file**
and `?src=URL`. It accepts:

- a `.trace.zip` package, or any `.zip` holding one TraceCite document;
- a `.trace.json` (any `.json` with `blocks`) on its own;
- a `.json` dropped together with its `.bib`, scripts and images. Files are
  matched by name to the paths the data names, then packed.

If a document needs files that are missing, it still opens, and the page says
what is missing: for example, an interactive's script.

The page shows each stage as it happens:

1. reading the file;
2. unzipping;
3. checking the manifest and version history;
4. preparing sources, maths, structure, cross-references, figures and
   interactives;
5. drawing.

If a document is already open, the new one replaces it, with a way back.
`scripts/zip.js` reads and writes zips with no dependencies, using
`CompressionStream` and `DecompressionStream`. `scripts/package.js` opens,
prepares and exports packages. Both run in browsers and in Node 20 or newer.

## One file that reads everything

`trace-reader.html` is a single, self-contained file. Everything happens in the
browser: BibTrace, maths tags, cross-references, environments, provenance,
citation styles and interactives. Readers need no Node, no builder and no
install. Download it from the
[latest release](https://github.com/prajwalsouza/TraceCite/releases/latest/download/trace-reader.html),
open it, and drop a package on it. Every release attaches it automatically,
with a sample package.

## Building (for authors)

```sh
# a reading page that carries its package (works opened from disk)
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data doc.trace.json --out doc.html
# also write the package, signing the new version
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data doc.trace.json --out doc.html --zip doc.trace.zip --by "Ada Example" --note "What changed"
# a page that fetches its package when served
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data doc.trace.json --out doc.html --data-url doc.trace.zip
# the standalone reader
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --reader --out trace-reader.html
```

The builder validates the data before packing it.

## Network use

Packages and the reader work offline. Google Fonts and MathJax load from their
CDNs when online. Offline, the system fonts are used, and TeX stays readable
as plain text. To render maths offline, bundle MathJax (`tex-svg.js`, about
2 MB) and point `MATHJAX` in `scripts/build-reading.mjs` at your copy.


---

<!-- docs/edits.md -->

# Edits: how a model streams edits into a TraceCite page

Runtime: `scripts/edits.js`, included in every reading page the builder makes (since 0.3.0).

A reading page can take edits while someone reads it. The model writes; the words appear in place, word by word;
the reader reviews each suggestion. **The page is the endpoint.** No server is required: anything that can run
script in the page (an agent with browser control, an extension, a test tool) talks to `window.TraceLive`.
A server that relays events is an optional transport, never a requirement: open the page with
`?edits-server=https://host` to have it listen to `<host>/events` and post requests and decisions to `<host>/inbox` and
`<host>/accepted`.

The page announces this in `<script type="application/json" id="trace-live-manifest">`. Look for it first.

## Before anything else: read what already happened

Every time you start (a new session, a new run, after any pause), check the page before you write anything:

```js
const mf = document.getElementById('trace-live-manifest')      // 1. is this page live-editable?
TraceLive.decisions                                             // 2. what the reader decided on earlier edits
TraceLive.decisionsSince(lastRunTime)                           //    or only what is new since you last looked
TraceLive.inbox.filter(r => r.status === 'open')                // 3. what the reader is waiting for
```

Each decision: `{ edit, decision: 'accepted' | 'rejected' | 'commented', op, target, result, before, text, by, req, at, comment? }`.

- **accepted**: that text is now the document. Build on it; never restore `before`.
- **rejected**: do not propose that edit again. If you try the same idea, change it.
- **commented**: the reader's `comment` asks you to revise that edit. Answer it with a new edit on the same target.

Only then answer the open requests. The page also fires `trace-live-decision` on `window` as decisions happen,
and remembers accepted edits across reloads in that browser.

## Read what the reader asked for

```js
TraceLive.inbox.filter(r => r.status === 'open')
// → [{ req, targets: ['s4'], selection: 'the gap between…', instruction: 'say this more simply',
//      onEdit: null | '<edit id>',   // set when the reader is commenting on one of your suggestions
//      blocks: [{ id, text }], at, status }]
```

The page also fires `trace-live-request` on `window` for each new request. Requests stay in that browser.

## Stream an edit

Whole edit, streamed by the page at writing pace (simplest):

```js
await TraceLive.stream({ op: 'replace', target: 's4', text: 'New sentence text…', by: 'Model name (agent)', req: 'r…' })
```

Or event by event, as your own tokens arrive:

```js
TraceLive.push({ type: 'focus',  target: 's4' })                       // optional: bring it into view
TraceLive.push({ type: 'begin',  edit: 'e1', op: 'replace', target: 's4', by: 'Model name (agent)', req: 'r…' })
TraceLive.push({ type: 'delta',  edit: 'e1', text: 'For each ' })      // as many as you like
TraceLive.push({ type: 'end',    edit: 'e1' })
TraceLive.push({ type: 'status', text: 'Reading section 2…' })         // optional, '' clears it
```

- `op`: `replace` (new text for the sentence) or `insert-after` (a new sentence after it).
- `target`: a sentence block id (`data-read-sentence` in the page, `id` in the trace data).
- `by`: always name yourself, and always as an agent: your model's name followed by `(agent)`, for example `"Example model (agent)"`. Accepted edits record
  `Added by / Edited by` with `via: agent`.
- `req`: the request you are answering, so it leaves the reader's waiting list.
- Text uses the trace format: `\( … \)` maths, `[words]{.tag-id}` spans, `[text](https://…)` links.
  Send each maths segment and each span whole in one delta (the page never shows half a formula).

## Rules

1. **Sentences only.** Never target citations, references, exact quotes or their passages; the page refuses them.
   A quote is the source's own words and stays verbatim.
2. **Every edit is a suggestion.** Nothing changes until the reader accepts it.
3. **One edit per idea.** Several small edits beat one long rewrite: the reader reviews them one by one.
4. **Keep the document's conventions:** its connected highlights (`hl-*` spans and `\class{hl-*}{…}` symbols),
   its tone, its terms.
5. A comment on your suggestion (`onEdit` set) asks you to revise it: stream a new edit for the same target.

## What the reader sees

- The old sentence struck through, the new words beside it, a caret while you write.
- A faint ruler of tick lines at the right edge, only while there is something to show (edits, or a tag in focus). The tick where an edit sits is darker;
  the tick being written to takes the accent colour and blinks. No dots, no other animation. Hovering a tick names
  the edit (beside the ruler when there is room, otherwise in the status line).
- A floating status line at the bottom centre: "Example model (agent) is writing…", "3 suggestions to review".
- **Review one by one** from that line (or a tick): Accept (A), Reject (R), Comment (C), previous/next (← →), Esc to stop.
  A comment is saved on the sentence as a suggestion comment (`Comment kind: suggestion`) and comes back to you as a request.
- **Edits** in the sidebar (under Tag tree) opens the edits view: every pending edit tinted, the current one stronger,
  with the review bar. Click Edits again or press Esc to leave it.
- The same ruler is a scroll track (click or drag to go anywhere; hovering names the section) and, while a tag is
  pinned or previewed, shows where its sentences are in that tag's colour.


---

<!-- docs/sample.md -->

# A sample that uses every part

`docs/sample/` holds one small TraceCite document that uses every part of the
format. Use it as a template, and as a reference for what each piece looks
like. It validates with no warnings:

```sh
node scripts/validate-trace.mjs docs/sample/sample.trace.json
```

Read it as a page:
[references/sample-reading.html](https://prajwalsouza.github.io/TraceCite/references/sample-reading.html).
Or download its package,
[samples/sample.trace.zip](../samples/sample.trace.zip), and drop it on
`trace-reader.html`.

## The files

```text
docs/sample/
├─ sample.trace.json       the document: one tree of blocks, its tags and front matter
├─ sample.bib              its sources in BibTrace: BibTeX plus trace-* evidence fields
└─ sample-interactive.js   one interactive component, registered with TraceViz.register
```

## The document: [sample.trace.json](sample/sample.trace.json)

| Part | Where in the sample | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Format and version | `format`, `version` | `"tracecite/1.0"`, and storage revision `2` |
| Front matter | `title`, `subtitle`, `eyebrow`, `authors`, `affiliations`, `date`, `revision`, `license`, `keywords` | The lines under the title |
| Sources | `bibliography: "sample.bib"`, `sources: []` | Sources live in BibTrace, and cite by entry key |
| Tag tree | `tagTree` | Role, support and topic families, and a `caption` tag |
| Connected highlights | `tagTree` → `connected` → `hl-n`, `hl-q` | `slot` colours, and `symbols` coloured in formulas |
| Parameters | `parameters` → `length-words` | A per-sentence measure, drawn as a strip |
| Sections | `sec-structure`, `sec-share` | `"Heading level": "2"`, and a span tag inside a heading |
| Sentences | `s-1` … `s-6` | Role and support tags, and a `Sentence review` field |
| Citation and exact reference | `s-1-c`, `s-1-c-r` | `Source ID`, and the quote it rests on |
| A comment and a reply | `s-2-n`, `s-2-n-r` | Note blocks with `Comment by` (a person, then an agent) |
| Interpretation | `s-3` | Labelled `role-interpretation`, with no source needed |
| Links | `s-3` | An external link (new tab) and an internal `#/at/sec-share` link |
| An environment | `p-def` | `env-definition`, with `Label` and `Name` fields |
| Maths | `s-4`, `s-5` | `\( p = q / n \)`, with `n` and `q` coloured |
| Span tags | `s-4`, `s-6`, `sec-share` | `[sentences]{.hl-n}`, `[checked quote]{.hl-q}` |
| An interactive figure | `fig-share` | `Interactive`, `Interactive settings`, and a caption paragraph |

## The sources: [sample.bib](sample/sample.bib)

Two BibTrace records, with passages checked verbatim:

- `raggett1999html`, the HTML 4.01 specification:
  - two quotes (`trace-quote`, `trace-quote-2`) that share one passage;
  - each quote's `-location`, `-context`, `-tags` and `-note-1`;
  - who added and checked them (`trace-quote-added-by`, `-checked-by`,
    `-checked-on`);
  - record-level `trace-added-by`, `-via` and `-on`, `trace-status`,
    `trace-checked` and `trace-url-read`.
- `tei2026guidelines`, the TEI P5 Guidelines: one quote with its passage, and
  a note signed by a person (`trace-quote-note-1-by`).

See [bibtrace.md](bibtrace.md) for every field.

## The package: sample.trace.zip

Building the sample, or exporting it from the reader, gives one zip:

```text
sample.trace.zip
├─ manifest.json            what is inside, and the version history
├─ sample.trace.json        the document, exactly as written
├─ sample.bib               its BibTrace sources
├─ sample-interactive.js    its interactive component
└─ assets/manuscript/…      figure images, when a figure names them in "Assets"
```

Its `manifest.json`:

```json
{
  "format": "tracecite/1.0",
  "package": 1,
  "version": 1,
  "title": "A small document that uses every part",
  "data": "sample.trace.json",
  "bibliography": ["sample.bib"],
  "assets": [],
  "interactiveScripts": ["sample-interactive.js"],
  "files": [
    { "path": "sample.trace.json", "bytes": 12268 },
    { "path": "sample.bib", "bytes": 5551 },
    { "path": "sample-interactive.js", "bytes": 1234 }
  ],
  "history": [
    { "version": 1, "date": "2026-11-25T00:00:00.000Z", "note": "First package",
      "hash": "sha256:f18843b7…", "previous": null }
  ],
  "generator": "TraceCite build-reading"
}
```

When the content changes, the next build adds version 2 to the history, with
the previous hash. [package.md](package.md) describes every field.

## Make your own from it

1. Copy `docs/sample/` and rename the files.
2. Replace the blocks, tags and sources with your own. Keep every quote
   verbatim, with the passage it sits in.
3. Validate it, then either drop the `.json` and `.bib` (and scripts) on
   `trace-reader.html` and Export a `.trace.zip`, or build a page:

```sh
node scripts/build-reading.mjs --data my.trace.json --out my.html --zip my.trace.zip
```
